beats.headline: Why are Java Enums actually classes?
beats.subline: Stop treating them like simple integer constants. They are powerful singletons.
beats.narration: Before Java 5, we used integers for constants, which was a type-safety nightmare. Today, Java enums are full-blown classes that extend java.lang.Enum. Let's see what the compiler actually builds.

beats.title: What javac generates

steps.explanation: Enums are final and extend Enum. You cannot extend other classes, but you can implement interfaces.
Each constant is a public static final instance created at class load time.

beats.narration: The compiler turns your enum into a final class. Each constant becomes a static singleton instance. This is why you can safely compare them with double-equals—it's just a reference check.

beats.title: Why == beats .equals()

top.label: Using .equals()
points: Throws NPE if status is null

beats.narration: Always use double-equals for enums. It is null-safe and catches type mismatches at compile time. If you compare an OrderStatus to a Permission, the code simply won't compile.

beats.title: The values() Trap
beats.subtitle: Performance warning for loops

nodes.label: Cache it
nodes.detail: Store in a List or array field

beats.narration: Calling values() creates a new array clone every single time to protect the internal state. In hot loops, cache the result once instead of calling it repeatedly.

beats.title: Part 1 Locked In
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 2): Attaching data and logic to your constants →
beats.narration: That is the foundation. In Part 2, we stop using parallel lookup tables and start attaching domain data directly to our enum constants.

beats.headline: Stop using parallel lookup tables.
beats.subline: Your enums can hold fields, constructors, and business logic.
beats.narration: Why maintain a separate map for enum codes? You can pack that data directly into the enum definition. Let's build a robust shipping method enum.

beats.title: Rich Enum Constants

steps.explanation: Pass initialization data directly to the constructor.
Always use private final fields to prevent shared mutable state.

beats.narration: Enum constructors are implicitly private. Always mark your fields private and final. Since enums are global singletons, mutable state is a recipe for thread-safety disasters.

beats.title: Constant-Specific Behavior

steps.explanation: Each constant implements the abstract method differently.
Forces every constant to provide its own implementation.

beats.narration: Need different behavior per constant? Define an abstract method. The compiler forces every constant to implement it, creating anonymous subclasses under the hood.

beats.title: O(1) Lookup Strategy
beats.caption: Avoid Enum.valueOf() for external codes

lines.text: // Use a static map for fast lookups
private static final Map<String, ShippingMethod> BY_CODE = ...

beats.narration: Don't use Enum.valueOf for external codes; it throws exceptions. Build a static map on startup to return an Optional. It is clean, fast, and safe.

beats.title: Part 2 Locked In
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 3): Modern switch expressions and exhaustiveness →
beats.narration: Data and logic are now inside the enum. In Part 3, we look at how modern switch expressions make your code bulletproof against future changes.

beats.headline: Your switch statement is a ticking time bomb.
beats.subline: Adding a new enum constant won't break your build—until it's too late.
beats.narration: Traditional switch statements are dangerous. If you add a new constant to your enum, the compiler stays silent while your logic silently fails. Let's fix that.

beats.title: Statement vs. Expression

bottom.label: Switch Expression

beats.narration: Switch expressions require every case to be handled. If you add a new enum constant, your build will immediately fail, forcing you to handle the new state. No more silent bugs.

beats.title: Java 21+ Pattern Matching

steps.explanation: Handle nulls explicitly in the switch expression.

beats.narration: Modern Java lets you handle nulls directly inside the switch. It is clean, readable, and keeps your logic centralized without extra null checks cluttering your methods.

beats.title: Switch Internals
beats.subtitle: How it works across modules
beats.narration: When switching across classes, the compiler generates a synthetic lookup array. This ensures that even if a library reorders constants, your switch still hits the correct branch.

beats.title: Part 3 Locked In
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 4): The ordinal() persistence trap →
beats.narration: Switch expressions are the gold standard. In Part 4, we discuss why saving ordinal values to your database is a critical architectural mistake.

beats.headline: Your database is lying to you.
beats.subline: Storing ordinal values in SQL will eventually corrupt your data.
beats.narration: Every enum has an ordinal—its declaration position. If you save that integer to a database, you are creating a time bomb. Let's see why.

beats.title: The Ordinal Shift
beats.subtitle: Adding a constant breaks history
beats.narration: If you insert a new constant in the middle, every subsequent constant shifts its ordinal. Your database records will suddenly map to the wrong status. Total disaster.

beats.title: Persistence Strategy
beats.narration: Always persist as a STRING or use a custom business code. String is human-readable and survives reordering. Never rely on the default ordinal mapping in JPA.

beats.title: The Business Code Pattern

steps.explanation: Use an explicit code field that never changes, even if the enum name changes.

beats.narration: For mission-critical data, use an explicit business code. It decouples your database from your Java source code, allowing you to refactor names without breaking your SQL records.

beats.title: Part 4 Locked In
beats.narration: Persistence solved. In Part 5, we wrap up with EnumSet and EnumMap—the hidden performance weapons for your collection handling.

beats.headline: Why use HashSet when you have bits?
beats.subline: EnumSet and EnumMap are the fastest collections in the JVM.
beats.narration: Stop using generic HashMaps for your enums. The standard library provides specialized collections that are faster, smaller, and cleaner. Let's see how they work.

beats.title: EnumSet: Bit Vectors

steps.explanation: Stores membership as bits in a long. No node allocations.

beats.narration: EnumSet is just a bit vector. For enums with under 64 constants, it uses a single long. Operations like contains are just bitwise checks. It is incredibly fast.

beats.title: EnumMap: Array Indexing

steps.explanation: Direct array access using ordinal() as the index.

beats.narration: EnumMap is even better. It uses a plain array indexed by the ordinal. No hash codes, no bucket collisions, and no entry objects. It is the most efficient map you can use.

beats.title: Performance Summary
beats.caption: When to use what
beats.narration: Use EnumSet and EnumMap by default for enum keys. They are faster, cleaner, and use less memory. Check out the roadmap link below for the full lab and tests.

beats.title: Chapter Complete
